newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's Bucaram warns Congress, showdown looms.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's Bucaram warns Congress, showdown looms.

text.p: Ecuador's President Abdala Bucaram, facing a possible congressional attempt to force him out of office, said on Thursday he would assume "all powers" necessary to quash any unconstitutional moves against him.

Bucaram, in an address to the nation, also announced he was shuffling his Cabinet and said he will reconsider the steep increases in the price of gas, electricity and other public services that ignited a wave of social protest and an ongoing general strike.
The speaker of Congress earlier called legislators to an extraordinary session where opponents were expected to debate the possible dismissal of the president, who took office in AUgust 1996.

But Bucaram said, "The government makes clear that in the case of an attempt to break with constitutional order, I will assume all the powers available to protect the legitimacy of the popular will and the national judicial order."
The government issued a statement saying the Congress session called for 6 p.m. EST (2300 GMT) was unconstitutional because it had not been advertised in local newspapers.

"Without such a statement having been published up to this morning, the speaker of Congress is assuring that there will be an extraordinary session to resolve the country's political crisis. If it proceeds in this way, it will be illegal and unconstitutional," the statement said.
In his address Bucaram said he was reconsidering the big hikes in gas and electricity prices that triggered a wave of social unrest, and was freezing fuel prices.

He also announced he had accepted the resignation of Energy and Mining Minister Alfredo Adum as part of a Cabinet shakeup. Government Minister Frank Vargas, Social Welfare Minister Adolfo Bucaram, who is the president's brother, and Administration Secretary Miguel Salem, were also leaving the government.
"I will carry out a broad renewal of officials and relations in order to tune in to the needs of the country," Bucaram said.
Unions earlier announced they had decided to indefinitely extend the 48-hour general strike they began Wednesday, saying they would continue to try to push Bucaram out of office.

"In a meeting at dawn, we decided to harden our stance and continue the strike until we achieve the dismissal of Abdala Bucaram," the Coordinating Board for Social Protests and the Indigenous Peoples Confederation said in a statement.

Social unrest erupted in the Andean country of 11.7 million people in January when the government launched an austerity package including hikes in electricity, telephone and public transportion rates.

Bucaram's tendency to name friends and family members to important posts and his flamboyant personality also irritated his opponents. Nicknamed "El Loco" -- "madman" in Spanish -- he released a rock-and-roll record soon after taking office and his antics included shaving his moustache off on live television.
A top Bucaram supporter said the government was lobbying Congress hard to avoid a vote to fire the president.
"We are putting together a majority. We are sure we are going to make it," said Monetary Board president Alvaro Noboa.

But one opposition congressman, Luis Macas, of the Pachakutik-New Country Party, said he was determined to vote to oust Bucaram, despite the president's warnings that he might assume extra powers if faced with a rebellious Congress.
"Our position is definitely to declare the post of president of Ecuador vacant," Macas told Reuters.
Of Congress's 82 members, 19 are members of Bucaram's Roldosista Party, while another 12 are government allies.
